title: Review: How enzymes work; Factors affecting enzyme activity; Enzyme inhibition and metabolic control; Experimental design and variables
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EZ03#t2 term and clue written for the game; EZ03#t3 term and clue written for the game; EZ01b#t1 term and clue written for the game; EZ03#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EZ01b#N.8b, EZ02#N.14a, EZ03#N.14, PR01a#N.6, EZ01b#N.6, EZ02#N.11a, PR01a#N.8, EZ01b#N.9, EZ02#N.3a, PR01a#N.10, EZ02#N.6a, PR01a#N.2a. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Active site
items.clue: Where the substrate normally binds; a molecule of similar shape can occupy it instead.

items.label: Tertiary structure
items.clue: Overall folding of an enzyme, altered when a molecule binds away from the substrate pocket.

items.label: Lock and key
items.clue: Fischer's 1894 model: a rigid binding pocket that only an exactly complementary substrate fits.

items.label: Competitive inhibitor
items.clue: Molecule similar in shape to the substrate that binds reversibly where the substrate should bind.

questions.stem: Trypsin is made by cells in the pancreas and digests proteins in the small intestine. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Trypsin is extracellular because it is made outside cells, in the pancreatic juice.
Trypsin is intracellular because proteins are digested inside the cells lining the small intestine.
Trypsin is extracellular: it is made inside pancreatic cells, secreted, and acts in the small intestine.
Trypsin is intracellular because it is made inside cells, like every enzyme.

questions.explanation: Made inside cells, secreted by exocytosis, acting outside cells: that is an extracellular enzyme.

questions.stem: An enzyme from a cold-water fish has an optimum temperature of about 15 °C. A sample was kept at 45 °C for 10 minutes and then cooled back to 15 °C. Its activity at 15 °C was only 5% of that of an unheated sample tested at the same time (illustrative data). Which explanation is correct?

options.text: The heat killed the enzyme molecules, so they no longer worked at 15 °C.
Heat broke bonds holding its shape; the active site changed and did not re-form.
At 15 °C the molecules moved too slowly to collide, so activity was low.
The heat broke its peptide bonds, splitting the enzyme into separate amino acids.

questions.explanation: At 45 °C hydrogen and ionic bonds broke and the active site lost its complementary shape. Cooling did not restore it: the enzyme was denatured.

questions.stem: Methanol is not very toxic itself, but the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase converts it into toxic products. Ethanol is also a substrate of alcohol dehydrogenase. Doctors have treated methanol poisoning by giving ethanol. Why does this reduce the harm?

options.text: Ethanol binds to an allosteric site, so the active site changes shape and methanol cannot bind.
Ethanol denatures alcohol dehydrogenase, so no methanol at all is converted.
Ethanol competes with methanol for the active site, so less methanol is converted at a time.
Ethanol binds to methanol molecules, so less methanol is free to reach the enzyme.

questions.stem: A student plans to test whether the number of double bonds in a fatty acid affects its melting point, using fatty acids with 0, 1, 2 and 3 double bonds that all have the same chain length. Which statement is an appropriate null hypothesis for this investigation?

options.text: Fatty acids with more double bonds will melt at lower temperatures than those with fewer.
Fatty acids with more double bonds will melt at higher temperatures than those with fewer.
The number of double bonds in a fatty acid has no effect on its melting point.
None of the fatty acids will melt at any of the temperatures used in the investigation.

questions.stem: According to the induced-fit model, what happens when a substrate binds to the active site of an enzyme?

options.text: Both the enzyme and the substrate change shape as they bind.
The rigid active site admits only an exactly matching substrate.
The active site closes around a substrate that keeps its shape.
The enzyme seizes the substrate and holds it without any changes.

questions.explanation: Both change shape when binding occurs. The closer fit strains bonds within the substrate, which is part of how catalysis is achieved.

questions.stem: At high substrate concentrations, the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction levels off even when more substrate is added. Why?

options.text: The enzyme molecules have been used up by the reaction, so no more product can be formed.
Every active site is occupied almost all the time, so extra substrate finds no free site to bind.
The high concentration of substrate denatures the enzyme, so its active site stops working.
The amount of energy the enzyme can supply each second has reached its upper limit.

questions.explanation: At saturation, as soon as one product leaves an active site another substrate binds. Adding substrate cannot increase the frequency of productive collisions further.

questions.stem: A filter-paper disc soaked in catalase solution sinks in hydrogen peroxide and rises when enough oxygen has formed on it. In 1% hydrogen peroxide the disc took 50 s to rise; in 2% it took 20 s. Which statement about the reaction rate is correct?

options.text: Rate is proportional to 1/time, so the rate at 2% (0.05 s⁻¹) is 2.5 times the rate at 1% (0.02 s⁻¹).
The rate at 1% is 50 and at 2% is 20, so the rate fell when the concentration was doubled.
Doubling the concentration doubles the rate, so the rate at 2% is 0.04 s⁻¹, twice that at 1%.
The rate cannot be found, because the volume of oxygen produced was not measured in either trial.

questions.stem: Hexokinase is the enzyme that adds a phosphate group to glucose. X-ray structures show that the two halves of the enzyme are further apart when no glucose is bound. When glucose binds, the two halves close around it. What does this evidence show?

options.text: It supports the lock-and-key model, as glucose fits an active site of fixed shape.
It shows that glucose denatures hexokinase, because the shape of the enzyme changes.
It shows the lock-and-key model was worthless, as it explained nothing about enzymes.
It supports the induced-fit model: the active site changes shape as substrate binds.

questions.stem: Catalase was added to hydrogen peroxide and the volume of oxygen collected was recorded: 0 s, 0 cm³; 20 s, 12 cm³; 40 s, 20 cm³; 60 s, 24 cm³ (illustrative data). What is the best estimate of the initial rate of reaction from these data?

options.text: 0.4 cm³ s⁻¹
20 seconds
0.60 cm³ s⁻¹

questions.explanation: 12 cm³ of oxygen in the first 20 s gives 12 ÷ 20 = 0.60 cm³ s⁻¹. With readings every 20 s, this first-interval rate is the best estimate the data allow.

questions.stem: Ecologists want to test the hypothesis that two limpet species compete for algae on a shore. Which approach tests the hypothesis by experiment rather than by observation?

options.text: Removing one limpet species from marked plots and recording the growth of the other over a year.
Recording the abundance of both limpet species in quadrats placed at random positions along the shore.
Measuring the shell sizes of both limpet species in laboratory tanks of seawater collected from the shore.
Applying a chi-squared test to records of where each species occurred in past shore surveys.

questions.stem: A student measured the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction at six temperatures. The rates, in arbitrary units, were: 10 °C, 2; 20 °C, 4; 30 °C, 8; 40 °C, 15; 50 °C, 9; 60 °C, 1 (illustrative data). Which conclusion is supported by these data?

options.text: The low rate at 10 °C shows that the enzyme had been denatured by the cold temperature.
The true optimum is 37 °C, the body temperature at which every enzyme works at its best.
The optimum is near 40 °C; above it, denaturation outweighs the faster collisions.
The fall in rate after 40 °C shows that the substrate had been used up at higher temperatures.

questions.stem: A student places a lamp at different distances from a beaker of pondweed in sodium hydrogencarbonate solution kept at 25 °C, and counts the bubbles of gas released per minute at each distance. Which correctly identifies the variables?

options.text: Independent: lamp distance; dependent: bubbles per minute
Independent: bubbles per minute; dependent: distance of lamp
Controlled variable: lamp distance; dependent: bubbles per minute
Independent: temperature of 25 °C; dependent: bubbles per minute

questions.explanation: The lamp distance is what the student deliberately changes (it sets the light intensity), so it is the independent variable; the bubble count is measured to find the effect, so it is the dependent variable. Temperature and hydrogencarbonate concentration are controlled variables.
